chapters.title: Chapter 2: The Statistical Toolkit — Correlation, Spread, and Z-Score

lessons.title: Correlation Between Two Stocks: What It Tells You and What It Doesn't

children.text: A friend messages you two ticker symbols and one number: "92% correlation over the last two years, this has to be a great pair." Before agreeing or disagreeing, you need to ask a question he probably has not: correlation between what, exactly, computed how? Correlation is the most commonly cited statistic in this entire field, and it is also the most commonly misused. This lesson is about learning exactly what a correlation number can tell you, and, just as importantly, the specific things it cannot.

body.text: Correlation measures how closely two return series have moved together over a specific sample period. It says nothing on its own about whether the prices of those two securities will ever converge, which is the actual question a stat arb trade depends on.

children.text: The Pearson correlation coefficient, the version almost everyone means when they say "correlation", measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two series. It is bounded between -1 and +1. A value near +1 means the two series tend to move in the same direction by proportional amounts. A value near -1 means they tend to move in opposite directions. A value near 0 means there is no meaningful linear relationship between their movements at all.

body.caption: x and y here should be the two stocks' returns, not their raw prices, for reasons the next section makes concrete.

children.text: The Rule Most Beginners Miss: Correlate Returns, Not Prices

markDefs.definition: A misleadingly high correlation between two series that share no real underlying relationship, often arising when both are computed on trending price levels rather than returns.

children.text: Here is the trap almost every beginner falls into at least once: computing correlation on raw price levels instead of returns. Two stocks can have almost nothing to do with each other economically and still show a price-level correlation above 0.9, purely because both happen to be in a long-term uptrend. This is a well known statistical trap called

. The correlation is not lying to you technically, but it is answering a nearly useless question, whether two series share a similar overall direction over this window, instead of the question you actually care about, whether the two move together day to day in a way that reflects a real, ongoing relationship.

body.text: Whenever a stat arb pair is pitched with a single headline correlation number and no mention of whether it was computed on prices or returns, assume prices until proven otherwise, and be skeptical. This exact trap, two trending series looking related purely because both trend, is also why Chapter 3 does not stop at correlation and introduces formal stationarity and cointegration tests instead.

children.text: What Correlation Tells You, and What It Doesn't

body.title: The Limits of a Correlation Number

columns.label: What Correlation Tells You
points: How strongly two return series moved together, in a straight-line sense, over the sample period measured
The direction of that co-movement (same direction vs opposite direction)
A reasonable first screen for shortlisting candidate pairs to investigate further

columns.label: What Correlation Does NOT Tell You
points: Whether the spread between the two prices reverts to a stable mean (a separate question, covered by cointegration testing in Chapter 3)
The correct hedge ratio, or how many shares of one to hold against the other (covered in Lesson 6)
Whether the relationship will keep holding going forward; correlation is backward-looking and can shift
Anything reliable at all, if it was computed on price levels rather than returns

children.text: Correlation Isn't Stable: A Rolling View

markDefs.definition: Correlation recalculated repeatedly over a moving window, for example the trailing 60 trading days, recomputed each new day, and plotted over time to see whether the relationship has stayed stable.

children.text: A single correlation number computed over three years of data can hide a lot. The relationship might have been strong for two and a half of those years and fallen apart for six months in the middle, and the full-sample average would never tell you that. A
, recalculated over a moving window such as the trailing 60 trading days, is a simple way to check whether a relationship has actually stayed stable, rather than trusting one summary statistic.

body.title: 60-day rolling correlation between two auto stocks over a year (illustrative)

body.text: The dip around months 4 to 6 is exactly the kind of thing a single full-sample correlation number would hide. Before trading this pair, you would want to know what happened during those months, a one-off stock-specific event, or a sign the relationship is genuinely less stable than the headline correlation suggests.

body.title: Which correlation actually matters?
body.question: Two stocks show a price-level correlation of 0.97 computed over the last three years. Both have also been in a steady long-term uptrend over that period. What should you check before treating this as evidence of a strong trading relationship?
options: Nothing, a correlation above 0.9 is always strong evidence of a tradeable pair
The correlation of their daily returns over the same period, since price-level correlation can be misleadingly high for two unrelated trending series
Whether both stocks are listed on the NSE
Whether the two stocks are in the same Nifty sectoral index
body.explanation: Price-level correlation between two trending series can look very high even when the two have no real economic relationship, simply because both are moving in the same broad direction. Return correlation strips out the shared trend and reveals whether the two actually move together day to day.

body.title: Reading a rolling correlation chart
body.scenario: You compute the 60-day rolling correlation between two auto stocks over the past year. It sits around 0.85 for most of the year, but drops to 0.35 for a six-week stretch in the middle, before climbing back to 0.85.
body.prompt: What would you want to find out about that six-week stretch before deciding whether this pair is reliable enough to trade?
body.modelAnswer: You would want to know what happened during those six weeks specifically: was there a stock-specific event, a product recall, a management change, a one-off regulatory issue, that temporarily broke the usual relationship, or does the relationship structurally weaken periodically for a reason that could recur? A single explainable, one-off dip is less concerning than a pattern of instability, and either way, you would want to check how the pair performs on formal statistical tests (Chapter 3) rather than relying on the rolling correlation chart alone.

cards.definition: A statistic between -1 and +1 measuring the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two series, most usefully computed on returns rather than price levels.
A misleadingly high correlation between two series that share no real underlying relationship, often arising when both are computed on trending price levels rather than returns.

Correlation recalculated repeatedly over a moving window, such as the trailing 60 trading days, used to check whether a relationship has stayed stable over time rather than relying on one full-sample number.

points: Correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two return series, bounded between -1 and +1.

Correlation should be computed on returns, not raw price levels. Two unrelated trending series can show misleadingly high price-level correlation while their actual day-to-day returns are barely related.

A high return correlation is a useful first screen for candidate pairs, but it does not tell you whether the pair's spread reverts to a stable mean. That is a separate, more demanding statistical question covered in Chapter 3.
Correlation is not stable over time. A rolling correlation over a moving window can reveal instability that a single full-sample correlation number hides.
A correlation number without knowing whether it was computed on prices or returns, and over what sample period, tells you very little on its own.
